summary:
Zephaniah prophesied "in the days of Josiah son of Amon king of Judah" (1:1), about 640–609 BC. His ancestry is traced four generations back to a Hezekiah — many take this to be King Hezekiah, though the text does not say. The sins he names — a "remnant of Baal," rooftop worship of "the host of heaven" (the stars), oaths sworn by the LORD and by Milcom, the god of Ammon (1:4–5) — are what Josiah's reforms removed in 622 BC (2 Kings 23), so the book is usually placed before the reforms or early in them. It also predicts the destruction of Nineveh, Assyria's capital (2:13), which fell to the Babylonians and Medes in 612 BC.

His theme is the Day of the LORD, the prophets' term for a time when God intervenes in judgment. The book opens, "I will completely sweep away everything from the face of the earth" (1:2) — man, beast, birds, fish, the creation order of Genesis 1 reversed. Then Jerusalem: God will search "with lamps" for the complacent who say, "The LORD will do nothing, either good or bad" (1:12). That day is "a day of wrath, a day of trouble and distress, a day of destruction and desolation" (1:15) — in the Latin Vulgate the verse begins "Dies irae, dies illa," the opening line the medieval hymn borrowed. Chapter 2 offers one shelter, "Seek righteousness; seek humility. Perhaps you will be sheltered on the day of the LORD's anger" (2:3), then pronounces judgment on the surrounding nations: Philistia, Moab and Ammon, Cush (south of Egypt), and Assyria (2:4–15).

Chapter 3 indicts Jerusalem's own leaders: her princes are "roaring lions," her judges "evening wolves," her prophets "reckless, faithless men," her priests "profane the sanctuary" (3:3–4). After judgment God promises "a meek and humble people" (3:12), "pure lips" for the peoples (3:9), and a song over the restored city: "The LORD your God is among you; He is mighty to save. He will rejoice over you with gladness; He will quiet you with His love; He will rejoice over you with singing" (3:17). The New Testament applies its central phrase to the return of Christ: "the Day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night" (1 Thessalonians 5:2).
